papers.abstract: The throughput of an LLM training job depends on its recipe: how the model is split across GPUs, how memory is traded for compute, and which kernels and communication overlaps it uses. The best recipe changes with every model, accelerator and framework version. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, so they miss levers outside that space and can ship a configuration that silently changes training. ATTUNE is a coding agent that tunes any working recipe unattended within a GPU-hour budget. Guided by a skill of search rules, scripts and lessons from past tuning campaigns, it diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time. A correctness gate outside the agent refuses any argument known to change the training objective. ATTUNE tunes Amazon's production post-training recipes on H100, H200 and B200 clusters, raising throughput by 1.7x on average. It beats the published throughput of four of NVIDIA's own benchmark recipes on NVIDIA's AutoModel framework by 6-17%. On models held out from its development, it improves the strongest public recipes most where they were written for another setting, by up to 2.6x on MiniMax-M2, and least where the vendor tuned them for the same hardware. Given the same GPU-hour budget, it outperforms existing automated tuners, including Bayesian optimization, random search and OptiCo, a recent LLM-agent tuner. Its gain on GLM-4.5 is more than four times the best alternative's. The same coding agent without ATTUNE's skill gains less and fails half its launches. deep_reading.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
deep_reading.content:
Move the same model to a different GPU or framework version, and the training recipe that was tuned for it may no longer be the fastest. ATTUNE, from Amazon, hands recipe tuning to a coding agent. Starting from any working recipe, it searches unattended within a GPU-hour budget the user sets, changing one lever at a time. ==What makes the result usable is a correctness gate outside the agent==: any argument that changes the training objective is refused before launch. Amazon's production post-training SFT recipes on H100, H200 and B200 get 1.7× faster on average and up to 3.9×. On four of NVIDIA's own AutoModel benchmark recipes, ATTUNE beats NVIDIA's published throughput by 6–17%. On MiniMax-M2, a model held out from development, throughput rises 2.6×.

![ATTUNE's architecture: (1) a single coding agent searches in a hypothesis–launch–profile–diagnose loop; (2) deterministic gates outside the agent refuse objective-changing flags, decide whether a measurement is valid and whether a candidate beats the leader, and re-check the leader before shipping; (3) the harness keeps the loop unattended; (4) a durable ledger records every run so a campaign can resume after a crash; (5) the skill passes the lever catalog and past lessons to later campaigns.](figs/2610.17528/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: throughput fixed knobs cannot reach, and "it runs" is not "it is unchanged"

A training recipe covers how the model is split across GPUs (TP, PP, EP, CP, DP), how much recomputation trades for memory, which kernels run and how communication overlaps. Existing automated tuners come in two kinds. Parallelization planners and vendor autoconfigurators search a fixed space with a cost model or a sweep. Black-box search such as Bayesian optimization needs no system model but many costly trial runs. Recent LLM-agent tuners such as OptiCo read profiles, but they too can change only a fixed list of knobs.

Two observations drive the design. First, the throughput a recipe misses lies partly in levers that only pay off when **changed together**, and partly in levers a fixed list **does not include at all**, such as virtual pipeline stages or a different expert dispatcher. Second, some configurations quietly change what is trained while the job still completes. The MoE expert capacity factor is a standard throughput argument, but it drops tokens that overflow an expert. `--grad-reduce-in-bf16` reads like a communication flag, but it also disables FP32 gradient accumulation. A tuner that only checks whether a job runs could ship either as an optimization.

## 2. Method: one agent searches, deterministic code judges

**Measurement.** One tuning session is a campaign: one model, one cluster, a fixed GPU count. Across candidates, the model, data, sequence length, global batch, precision and GPU count stay fixed, and every run reads the same rows in the same order. Each run lasts a fixed number of steps. The first steps absorb startup and compilation and are not scored; the remaining window $W$ is scored by aggregate throughput:

$$s(x)=\frac{\sum_{i\in W}\text{tokens}_i}{|G|\sum_{i\in W}\text{stepTime}_i}$$

Summing before dividing keeps short steps from weighing too much. The baseline runs at least five times on different node allocations; its mean is the denominator, and the noise band is $\max(3\%, 3\sigma)$. A candidate replaces the leader only if it beats it by more than the band.

**Search discipline.** The agent uses ordinary tools: file search and reading (including the framework source in the training image), a shell and the cluster API. The skill sets six rules. State a hypothesis before each launch (which bottleneck shrinks, the mechanism, the expected gain). Change one lever, or one coupled set of parallelism degrees, per candidate. Before using a flag, read its implementation in the running image, including what it asserts and which flags it silently overrides, and record the code location in the ledger. Rule out a lever only after measuring two of its values or reaching its feasible limit, and call topology exhausted only after probing all five parallelism degrees. When trying a new layout, start without the leader's memory savings and add them back if it runs out of memory. Once the layout settles, re-test flags that won on earlier layouts.

**Diagnosis.** The agent mainly reads step time, per-stage memory and step-time variance within the window. When the bottleneck is unclear it profiles a run, tracing one rank per pipeline stage, and a deterministic trace analyzer splits each step into compute, communication, host-side and idle time.

**Control plane and budget.** To launch a candidate, a run generator copies the baseline job and changes only the flags and allowlisted environment variables under test. An accounting script charges GPU-hours from scheduler admission to release, including failed runs and correctness checks, and admits a launch only if it fits the remaining budget. The control plane also refuses to relaunch a recipe that failed, forcing the agent to diagnose and change it.

**Correctness gate.** The gate has two steps. Before launch, a configuration check compares the candidate's **resolved** arguments and environment with the baseline's (resolved values, because one flag can silently change others) and classifies each change in a registry no tuner can edit. "Known invalid" changes alter what is trained (data, batch, optimizer or its schedule, a loss term, routing, precision format) or trigger a known stack defect, and they are refused. "Known valid" changes alter only how the computation runs (placement, packing, or a same-math swap such as a fused kernel that matches an FP32 reference on identical inputs), and they pass. Everything else is "unknown": it goes on to the loss check and is listed in the report for review. After the run, the loss check requires the step-0 loss to be within 5% of the baseline's and every logged loss to be finite. Step 0 applies the same weights to the same first batch before any update, so a legitimate change moves it only through floating-point evaluation order, while wrong weight loading or sharding moves it by multiples.

**Unattended operation.** The harness builds on Claude Code's persistent-goal feature. A stop hook keeps the agent from ending its turn until the budget is spent or a stop is recorded with evidence. A pre-tool hook turns any question to the user into "take the default and record the assumption", and blocks unrecognized destructive shell commands. An append-only ledger is the single source of truth, so a fresh session can rebuild the campaign. At the end, the agent writes a summary and lessons, which enter the skill after human review.

## 3. Core contribution

The main contribution is the split of responsibilities: **an open action space for the agent, and the verdicts kept in deterministic code**. The agent may change any argument the framework exposes unless the gate marks it as objective-changing. Which measurements count, which candidate leads and which recipe ships are all decided by scripts the agent cannot edit. The authors also release OpenRecipes, a leaderboard of more than 60 recipes for more than 20 models, measured under one protocol (8,192-token SFT rows, global batch 128, BF16). Each entry lists tokens/s/GPU and cost per million tokens, and has passed Megatron-Bridge's convergence check.

## 4. Experiments

**Against the strongest public recipes.** There are two sets. The reproduced set is NVIDIA's four AutoModel benchmark recipes, run unchanged in NVIDIA's container on the H100s they target; three come within 2% of the published figures. The ported set is four models held out from development, trained on real text on slime and Megatron-LM.

| Model | GPUs | Baseline (tok/s/GPU) | ATTUNE | Gain | MFU (%) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 8×H100 | 11,963.1 | 13,151.1 | +9.9% | 27.9→30.7 |
| GPT-OSS-20B | 8×H100 | 12,970.3 | 15,222.5 | +17.4% | 30.1→35.3 |
| Llama-3.1-70B | 64×H100 | 801.2 | 1,012.5 | +26.4% | 36.4→46.0 |
| GLM-4.5 | 128×B200 | 723.6 | 969.0 | +33.9% | 7.2→9.7 |
| MiniMax-M2 | 64×B200 | 895.2 | 2,365.1 | +164.2% | 3.2→8.5 |
| Llama-3.1-405B | 128×B200 | 394.9 | 421.9 | +6.8% | 22.2→23.7 |
| Mixtral-8x22B | 128×H100 | 1,072.4 | 1,072.4 | 0.0% | 26.3 |

The size of the gain depends on how far the original recipe is from the current setting. MiniMax-M2's recipe was written for RL on 128 GPUs with optimizer state in CPU memory; all three campaigns turned CPU offload off and deepened the pipeline. GLM-4.5's recipe was written for H100; on B200 it was diagnosed as bound by communication and kernel launches, so the expert all-to-all moved inside a node, and the fastest campaign also dropped TP to 1. Llama-3.1-70B dropped context parallelism and switched to FlashAttention-3, reaching a step that is 98.5% compute. The Mixtral and 405B recipes are vendor benchmarks for the same hardware and leave little room; Mixtral's best candidate stayed within the noise band, so the original recipe was kept.

**Against other tuners on the same budget.** Every tuner gets 30× the cost of one baseline run in GPU-hours, the same gate and the same shipping rule, with three campaigns per model. On GLM-4.5, ATTUNE averages +33.9% using 669 GPU-hours and 6.4 hours; OptiCo gets 0.0% (1,407 GPU-hours), random search +7.8% (1,688), BO +1.8%, and BO with a memory pre-filter +3.9%. On MiniMax-M2, ATTUNE reaches +164.2% against +55.5% for the best rival, BO with the pre-filter. Notably, ATTUNE's fastest GLM-4.5 layout (minus virtual stages) lies inside OptiCo's 11-knob schema and is within 2% of ATTUNE's recipe, but OptiCo never reached it: it tried TP=1 only with shallower pipelines and with EP still crossing nodes. The black-box searches had every winning lever in their space but no diagnosis to guide them; most draws ran out of memory or were pruned as slower than the leader.

![Best-so-far gain versus cumulative GPU-hours on GLM-4.5 / 128×B200 (line: mean of three campaigns; shading: range). ATTUNE passes +20% within the first 30% of the budget and stops well before the 1,880 GPU-hour budget.](figs/2610.17528/hf2.png)

**Ablations.** On GLM-4.7-Flash and Nemotron-3-Nano (8×H200, five campaigns per arm): without the skill, mean gain falls from +88.0% to +66.9% and from +49.4% to +42.9%, and failed launches rise to 50%. Restricted to OptiCo's knobs, GLM-4.7-Flash gets only +18.1%, because its biggest win is turning off CPU optimizer offload, which is not on the list. Without logs and profiles, gains are slightly lower but not significantly (p = 0.24 and 0.14).

**The gate itself.** On runs with a known answer, all 460 legitimate runs pass, and every configuration fault is refused before launch. Of six code faults, the two that change the forward pass raise the step-0 loss by more than 150% and are caught. Faults that act only through the update (such as skipping one gradient bucket's reduction) are invisible at step 0, and a loss mask shifted by one token moves the loss by only 2.0%, about as much as the largest legitimate change; these pass. In real campaigns, the configuration check refused 19 uneven pipeline splits on Nemotron-3-Nano. One of them was the fastest run: it loaded another layer's weights into the Mamba layers, with a step-0 loss 215–768% above baseline.

## 5. Limitations

The authors list three. The gate sees only the configuration and step 0, so faults acting only through optimizer updates go undetected, and a full training run is still needed before production. The lever catalog comes from past campaigns, and GLM-4.5 shares a family with the development model GLM-5.2, so some gain may come from priors; however, without the catalog GLM-4.5 lands within the same noise band as full ATTUNE. ATTUNE tunes only what the framework and image expose, not kernels or code, and does not cover RL rollout. The lessons also need curation: on review, about a fifth of the catalog entries were wrong, and some held only on the workload where they were measured.

## 6. What it means in practice

For training-platform teams, the gate and the accounting are worth borrowing more than the agent itself. Whether tuning is done by people or by an agent, you can build a check that diffs resolved arguments, uses a non-editable valid/invalid registry and compares step-0 loss, so that flags like capacity factor or bf16 gradient reduction, which quietly change the objective, are stopped before launch. Charge the budget from scheduler admission to release, failed runs included. Automated tuning pays most when a recipe was ported from other hardware or another task (such as RL). With a vendor benchmark recipe tuned for the same hardware, expect much less; such recipes gained 0–26% in the paper. Review the lesson library against the raw records periodically, and keep only entries the model does not already know or that correct its wrong intuitions.

papers.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
papers.abstract: Data-intensive GPU applications increasingly rely on NVMe SSDs to extend GPU memory. NVIDIA GPU Direct Storage (GDS) enables direct SSD-GPU transfers via PCIe peer-to-peer DMA, eliminating host staging. However, GDS retains three key limitations: (1) its control path traverses the kernel for every I/O request, introducing software overhead; (2) its stream-ordered path imposes strict total ordering even when workloads only require batch-level ordering; and (3) its closed-source user-space engine hinders diagnosis and custom scheduling. We present uGDS, https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/uGDS, an open-source user-space GPU Direct Storage library built on four principles: user-space control, unified cross-vendor abstraction, workload-aware scheduling, and end-to-end transparency. The host CPU manages the entire NVMe command lifecycle in user space, while payloads move via PCIe P2P DMA without consuming GPU compute. A minimal kernel module (ugds_drv.ko) is used only for one-time privileged setup. uGDS partitions hardware queues between synchronous and batch traffic, enforces DMA-safe buffer lifetimes, and provides cuFile-compatible synchronous, batched, and stream-ordered APIs with polling or interrupt completion on both NVIDIA CUDA and AMD HIP. Evaluated on an A100 with a Samsung 990 PRO, uGDS achieves up to 12.12x GDS's batch-read bandwidth and 30.69x its batch-write bandwidth (8- and 4-KiB requests, batch size 128), and reduces 4-KiB synchronous write latency by 84.1% with two threads. Its stream-ordered path sustains 5.49 GiB/s on a single stream, where GDS retains only 40.8% of its synchronous bandwidth. In LMCache, uGDS reduces median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by up to 62.7% and raises serving goodput by 2.63x. On AMD, uGDS achieves up to 1.19x hipFile's synchronous-write bandwidth.

## 1. The problem: the data no longer detours, but control still does

GDS fixed the **data path**: the SSD reads and writes GPU memory directly through PCIe P2P DMA, with no staging in host memory. But its **control path** still enters the kernel on every I/O. Each cuFile call traverses VFS, the filesystem, the block layer and the kernel NVMe driver, and the nvidia-fs module intercepts each request's DMA mapping to translate every 4-KiB shadow page into a cached GPU bus address. Large transfers amortize this fixed cost; for the small, latency-sensitive requests common in KV-cache offloading and vector-index lookups, it becomes the main cost.

The authors identify two more gaps. One is **over-strict ordering**: cuFile's stream-ordered APIs inherit CUDA stream FIFO semantics, so every request is ordered after the previous one. Yet when LMCache restores a prefix, its chunks need no order among themselves; only the attention kernel must wait for all of them. Applications end up spreading I/O over many streams, doing the library's scheduling themselves. The other is **opacity**: the nvidia-fs kernel module is open source, but libcufile, which implements batch submission, worker threads and stream integration, ships only as a binary, so stalls can be neither inspected nor fixed by changing the scheduling policy. Earlier user-space prototypes such as libnvm/ssd-gpu-dma showed the approach is feasible, but they support only NVIDIA, assume a single submitter in their queue primitives, and do not track in-flight commands, so a buffer can be freed while the SSD is still writing into it.

## 2. Method: the CPU orchestrates, the SSD transfers, the GPU computes

**Three separated paths.** At setup, the application talks to ugds_drv.ko through a character device (open, mmap, ioctl): it claims the NVMe PCI device, maps the BAR0 controller registers and queue memory into the process, pins GPU memory across vendors, and optionally sets up an MSI-X interrupt bridge. During steady-state I/O the kernel module is not involved at all: libugds.so fills 64-byte NVMe submission entries (SQEs) in user space, builds PRP page lists, writes the mapped doorbell registers directly, and polls the completion queue (CQEs). Data flows only between SSD and GPU memory. The cost is that the SSD must be unbound from the kernel NVMe driver, and applications see block-device offsets rather than POSIX files. The authors argue this fits storage engines such as LMCache and Mooncake, which manage their own chunk pools; a user-space filesystem can sit on top when file semantics are needed.

**Request translation.** With logical block size $B$, a request must satisfy $\mathit{offset} \bmod B = 0$ and $\mathit{size} \bmod B = 0$, and the command fields are $\mathit{LBA}=\mathit{offset}/B$ and $\mathit{NLB}=\mathit{size}/B-1$. A contiguous chunk of size $C$ needs $P=\lceil C/S \rceil$ page descriptors ($S$ is the controller page size): one page uses PRP1, two use PRP1+PRP2, and beyond that PRP2 points to a host-side page list. The synchronous path pre-maps one PRP-list page per queue pair (QP); larger requests are split by MDTS, or conservatively at 128 KiB when the controller advertises no MDTS. Memory fences before the doorbell write make sure the PRPs and SQE are visible to PCIe.

**Cross-vendor GPU memory registration.** uGDSBufRegister() translates CUDA or HIP virtual pointers into a vendor-neutral array of controller-visible page addresses, recorded in a process-wide buffer registry; on NVIDIA, physical page tables come from the peer-memory API at 64-KiB granularity. Registered buffers can also be exported as DMA-bufs for RDMA NICs.

**Queue partitioning.** QPs are statically split into two domains: a general pool for synchronous and stream-ordered requests, and one dedicated deep queue for batch I/O only, so bursty batch submissions do not inflate synchronous queueing delay. Within the general pool, an atomic round-robin counter picks a QP, and a request holds that QP's lock from submission until its final CQE, so ring indices and doorbells need no extra atomics. The batch path coalesces many commands into one doorbell write to amortize MMIO cost. Stream-ordered requests attach a host callback via cudaLaunchHostFunc, and the callback calls the same user-space engine as synchronous reads and writes.

**DMA-safe lifetimes.** This is where user-space drivers most often go wrong. Before each I/O, the library atomically takes in-flight references on the device handle and target buffers; releasing a handle or buffer with transfers still in flight returns -EBUSY. Each registration carries a monotonically increasing generation token, so a stale request cannot unpin a new buffer that reuses a just-freed virtual address. On a command timeout, the handle is marked wedged, all further submissions are refused, and the affected QPs and memory are quarantined; forced reclamation is allowed only after an external controller reset (such as a PCIe Secondary Bus Reset) has stopped the DMA engine.

**Choice of completion mode.** The default is busy polling. MSI-X interrupts are also available: the kernel interrupt handler only signals an eventfd, and CQEs are still reaped in user space.

uGDS's value is not the idea of kernel bypass itself; user-space NVMe (such as SPDK) has existed for years. This matters for elastic serving that frequently spawns and recycles workers.

At batch size 128, GDS's first batch takes 90.84 ms for reads and 117.65 ms for writes, 87.7% and 92.2% of the whole 64-MiB transfer. nvidia-fs does not create the P2P mapping at registration but calls nvidia_p2p_dma_map_pages() on the first I/O; the authors suspect cuFile also lazily allocates batch state sized to the first submission. uGDS does all of this during setup, so its first batch matches later ones (2.46 vs 2.45 ms for reads). | Metric | GDS | uGDS |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median TTFT, 32,768-token prompt | 1915 ms | 715 ms |
| Goodput, 1,024-token prompts, concurrency 256 | ~19 kTokens/s (saturates at 32) | 50.2 kTokens/s |
| Median SSD→buffer transfer latency (concurrency 256) | 56.04 ms | 19.98 ms |
| Share of wall-clock in submission calls (async depth 64) | 99.6% | 1.0% |
| Single-stream 16-MiB async read bandwidth | 2.36 GiB/s | 5.49 GiB/s |

From 3,840 to 40,704 prompt tokens, TTFT falls a steady 2.45–2.68×. GPU-side scattering of KV into vLLM's paged memory takes the same time for both (0.189 vs 0.193 ms), so the gain comes entirely from the storage path.

uGDS must unbind the whole SSD from the kernel driver and gives up the filesystem, POSIX locks and page-cache coherence, so the drive cannot serve other processes as a normal disk. Each handle currently drives one local SSD; multi-SSD striping and NVMe-oF are on the roadmap. Synchronous requests get QPs round-robin and hold them until completion, so a large request can delay small requests on the same QP; the authors plan a load-aware scheduler. The experiments use one consumer 990 PRO, one A100 and IOMMU disabled, and the end-to-end test uses only the small Qwen3-0.6B; behavior with datacenter SSDs or many GPUs behind a shared PCIe switch remains to be shown.

## 6. What it means in practice

If you are building KV-cache tiering (HBM→DRAM→SSD) or GPU vector search on a dedicated local SSD, uGDS is worth testing as a GDS replacement, especially for small, frequent, single-stream reads, exactly where GDS suffers most. Before deploying, confirm three things: the SSD can be owned exclusively and unbound from the kernel driver; the layer above already manages its own block allocation (as LMCache and Mooncake do); and your IOMMU policy permits P2P. Choose completion mode per workload: busy polling for latency-sensitive inference nodes, MSI-X for throughput-bound or CPU-constrained pipelines. Even without switching libraries, the paper's analysis of GDS's lazy first-batch initialization and single-stream submission blocking is directly usable: warm up each buffer–device pair first, then spread critical reads over several streams.

papers.title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
papers.abstract: Head-dimension compression can reduce the memory required by the key-value (KV) cache, but existing methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations during inference, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead. We formalize the design considerations for converting pretrained attention into a natively reduced-dimensional form that reduces both KV-cache storage and attention computation using a calibration set. Specifically, we consider reductions that (1) apply a shared projection to queries and keys so that they remain in a common reduced feature space, (2) derive this projection jointly from query and key activations to better preserve their interaction, and (3) are compatible with the pretrained RoPE transformation. To obtain a reconstruction-free realization of this reduction, we restrict it to coordinate selection and theoretically show that RoPE compatibility then holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained. Building on this characterization, we introduce RACE, a post-training method that selects rotary pairs using their joint query-key activation energy. We theoretically show that this criterion minimizes a separable, calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into the model weights and require neither runtime reconstruction nor specialized kernels. Across three model families and different compression levels, RACE outperforms structured pruning and remains competitive with reconstruction-based methods on language-modeling, zero-shot, and long-context tasks. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, yielding 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory in comparison to an uncompressed model.

deep_reading.content:
KV cache size is tokens × layers × head dimension × precision. Cutting tokens (H2O, SnapKV) and cutting precision (KIVI) are well studied. Methods that cut the head dimension exist too, but most of them save only **storage**: EigenAttention and PALU store keys as low-dimensional vectors, then reconstruct full-dimensional keys at inference time so that RoPE positional encoding can be applied. The paper's Table 1 quantifies the cost: at 50% KV retention, EigenAttention's decode FLOPs are 11.42× those of standard attention and PALU's are 21.92×. RACE (RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression based on activation Energy) takes a different route: ==keep only complete RoPE rotary pairs, choose them by the joint activation energy of queries and keys, and fold the choice straight into the weights==. RoPE, caching and attention then all run in the reduced dimension, with no reconstruction and no custom kernel. On Llama-3.2-3B at 50% KV retention and 256K context, total inference FLOPs drop 47.8%, overall throughput rises 1.79×, time to first token (TTFT) falls 43.2% and GPU memory falls 28.1%.

![Left: RACE's "native" compression reduces dimensions before RoPE and folds them into W_Q and W_K, so all of attention runs in low dimension. Right: reconstruction-based methods cache low-dimensional representations but restore the full dimension with factor matrices A and B before computing (dashed boxes are full-dimensional operations).](figs/2610.28385/hf2.png)

## 1. The problem: storage saved, compute not

Why is head-dimension compression hard? Attention scores depend on $\tilde Q \tilde K^\top$ **after** RoPE. RoPE treats every two adjacent coordinates of a head as a "rotary pair" on a 2-D plane and rotates it by an angle that depends on token position. If a dense low-rank matrix projects keys to low dimension before RoPE, that projection generally does not commute with the rotation: projecting then rotating differs from rotating then projecting. Methods like EigenAttention and PALU must therefore rebuild full-dimensional keys before RoPE. PALU writes a custom kernel so the reconstructed tensor is never materialized, but decode FLOPs are still dominated by the reconstruction basis.

Two other approaches each miss a piece. Thin Keys avoids key reconstruction but leaves value dimensions untouched, so KV savings stop at 75% retention. The concurrent RAP also keeps complete rotary pairs, but scores them with empirical Fisher from gradients of $W_K$, which needs backpropagation and looks only at the key side.

The authors frame the task as **constrained approximate matrix multiplication**: find a low-dimensional map $P$ with $(\tilde Q P)(\tilde K P)^\top \approx \tilde Q \tilde K^\top$, subject to the map being executable before RoPE. Two design principles follow. Queries and keys should share one low-dimensional subspace, because their product is taken along the same feature dimension. And the subspace should be chosen from statistics of both queries and keys, because the quantity being approximated is their product.

## 2. Method: keep complete rotary pairs, rank them by joint energy

**Which reductions commute with RoPE?** Theorem 1 gives the exact answer for coordinate selection (keeping some coordinates and dropping the rest): it commutes with RoPE if and only if the kept coordinates form a union of **complete rotary pairs**, ordered consistently with the original RoPE. The intuition is direct. The two coordinates of a pair mix during rotation, so keeping only one of them loses the part mixed in from the other. When the condition holds, rotating the reduced vector by the original frequencies gives exactly the same result as rotating in full dimension and then selecting coordinates.

**Which pairs to keep?** For the $m$-th rotary pair of each attention head, compute the joint energy on calibration data:

$$E_m=\|Q_m\|_F^2+\|K_m\|_F^2$$

$Q_m$ and $K_m$ are the query and key activations of all calibration tokens on that pair of coordinates, and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm. For target dimension $r_k$, keep the $r_k/2$ pairs with the highest energy. Proposition 1 shows that the product error from dropping a set of pairs is bounded by $\frac12\sum E_m$ over the dropped pairs, so taking the top-energy pairs minimizes this separable bound exactly. The authors are explicit that this is not the same as minimizing the true error; it is a cheap, forward-only criterion.

**Values.** Values are not rotated, so RACE follows EigenAttention: run SVD on calibration activations and use the top $r_v$ right singular vectors as $P_V$.

**Folding into weights.** Once chosen, $W_Q$ and $W_K$ are right-multiplied by $P_{QK}$, $W_V$ by $P_V$, and $W_O$ is left-multiplied by $P_V^\top$. The result is an ordinary attention layer with a smaller head dimension. It caches low-dimensional K and V, applies RoPE only to the kept pairs (keeping their original frequency indices rather than renumbering them), and computes the QK dot product, value aggregation and output projection in low dimension with standard PyTorch attention.

Energies are computed on 32,768 calibration tokens, the top 32 pairs are kept, and the key dimension drops to 64; SVD also reduces values to 64. This layer's KV cache halves, QK and value-weighting compute each halve, and $W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O$ shrink with them.

The main contribution is deciding which compressions are legal. RACE starts from matrix-product approximation, uses forward statistics only, and looks at both queries and keys. Appendix Figure 12 plots approximation error per layer; joint Q/K selection is lower than one-sided selection in most layers.

A few implementation details are worth copying. Calibration statistics and SVD run in FP32 and inference in BF16. Kept rotary pairs retain their original frequency indices and RoPE scaling rules rather than being renumbered as consecutive frequencies. The attention scale stays at the original $1/\sqrt{d_k}$. ## 4. Experiments

**Quality at matched KV budgets.** The question is whether accuracy keeps up with reconstruction-based methods without reconstruction. | Method | Reconstruction-free | KV retained | Attn. params retained | Prefill FLOPs | Decode FLOPs |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| EigenAttention | No | 50% | 69.8% | ×0.75 | ×11.42 |
| PALU | No | 50% | 58.3% | ×0.75 | ×21.92 |
| Thin Keys | Yes | 75% | 50% | ×0.75 | ×0.75 |
| RAP | Yes | 50% | 50% | ×0.5 | ×0.5 |
| RACE | Yes | 50% | 50% | ×0.5 | ×0.5 |

![Quality-efficiency trade-off on Llama-3.2-3B. Left: mean zero-shot accuracy versus KV retention. Right: decode FLOPs (log scale, standard attention = 1). RACE's accuracy is close to reconstruction-based methods while its decode FLOPs match RAP's low cost; reconstruction methods sit an order of magnitude higher.](figs/2610.28385/hf1.png)

**System benefits.** The question is whether saved storage turns into lower compute and latency. Tests use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with 64K/128K/256K prompts and 128 output tokens, averaged over 10 runs. Gains grow with prompt length because attention takes a larger share of total cost. At 256K and 50% retention, prefill, decode and overall throughput improve 1.76×, 1.90× and 1.79×. Memory drops only 28.06% rather than half, because total memory also includes parameters and activations that RACE does not touch.

![Long-context efficiency at up to 256K prompts. Top row: prefill, decode and overall throughput speedups over the uncompressed model. Bottom row: TTFT, GPU memory and total FLOPs. The 50% retention setting gains most at 256K.](figs/2610.28385/hf11.png)

**Stacking with token compression and quantization.** Applying RACE at 75% and then H2O, SnapKV or KIVI at 50% each gives 37.5% total retention. Applying RACE to an already-compressed model costs more accuracy than applying it to the original, so the two compressions do not act independently. Stacking with KIVI quantization loses least, especially in perplexity.

Under aggressive compression the wide-head model holds up best, because wider heads offer more rotary pairs to choose from.

## 5. Limitations

The authors state that the energy criterion minimizes a separable upper bound, not the true error; 50% retention needs a distillation recovery step, so it is not fully training-free; and when stacked with token compression, the losses of the two stages compound. Theorem 1 covers only coordinate selection; to stay reconstruction-free the paper deliberately gives up more general dense low-rank projections, and it does not discuss whether a larger commuting family holds better solutions. In addition, system gains were measured on a single 3B model; gains below 256K are smaller, and the paper does not report what happens on large models or GQA architectures with very few KV heads.

For long-context serving, RACE is easy to deploy: the output is a standard checkpoint with a smaller head dimension, backends such as vLLM or SGLang need no kernel changes, and it stacks with KV quantization like KIVI. A sensible pilot is 75% retention on your own model, calibrated on about 30K tokens of generic text with no distillation, then checking long-document tasks for regressions. Going to 50% calls for one KL distillation pass on the order of 1M tokens. papers.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents can handle increasingly complex tasks, navigating long trajectories of observations and actions. As these trajectories grow, key-value (KV) cache I/O and storage become the dominant cost. Trajectories can also exceed the LLM's maximum context length, requiring control over active cache growth. Prior work uses context engineering to reduce cache size by trimming or summarizing history. However, modifying the trajectory prefix invalidates subsequent cached states and triggers costly re-prefilling of retained context. Task accuracy can also suffer when too little context is retained to limit re-prefill costs. We propose cache engineering as a new scheme. It allows agents to directly control their active KV cache without modifying the trajectory or re-prefilling retained context. Specifically, agents can proactively use drop to exclude selected cache from future attention and repos to adjust retained keys' position encodings. We formalize these cache operations and identify history dependence as a serving challenge: identical token sequences can yield different cache states under different cache operation sequences, making prefix matching insufficient for correct cache reuse. Thus, we co-design the AKV serving engine. It provides a stateless interface compatible with existing serving APIs, while internally managing stateful cache reuse, eviction, and restoration. Experiments show that a tool-response rolling-drop cache policy improves average benchmark scores by 1.7 points and reduces average cost by 27.7%, compared with conventional threshold-triggered summarization. With AKV, it achieves up to 1.2x the output throughput and a 1.5x speedup in P95 request latency. Recursive self-improvement of cache policies further reduces cost by 7.1% over expert design. Our code is at https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV.
papers.authors: Tianyu Fu, Ruoxi Wang, Zihan Min, Zhongqi Ren, Zhihao Li, Tengxuan Liu, Shengxu Mu, Hanling Zhang, Yu Wang

This paper shifts from rewriting history text to engineering cache lifetime and eviction. Versus threshold-triggered summarization, a simple tool-response drop policy cuts average cost 27.7% and lifts benchmark scores 1.7 points; with AKV it reaches ~1.2× output throughput and ~1.5× better P95 latency; an RSI policy saves another 7.1% on held-out tasks. KV reads can be 82.4% of API cost. ==Agent cost often turns on not invalidating cache, not only on shorter summaries==.

deep_reading.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
deep_reading.content:
Once an agent runs for hundreds of rounds, the dominant cost is no longer generation but repeatedly reading the historical KV cache: by the paper's count, KV cache reads account for 82.4% of total API cost. The usual remedy is context engineering, trimming or summarizing old messages, but editing the prefix invalidates every later cached state and forces a re-prefill. A Tsinghua team proposes **cache engineering**: leave the text trajectory untouched, drop selected entries directly from the active KV cache, and reuse what remains as is. With its serving system AKV, a simple tool-response rolling-drop policy across three models and four agent benchmarks ==raises average scores by 1.7 points and cuts average cost by 27.7%== relative to conventional threshold-triggered summarization, with 1.18× output throughput and a 1.51× speedup in P95 request latency.

![Full-context inference, context engineering and cache engineering. Full-context inference reuses all historical KV; context engineering removes irrelevant text and recomputes the retained history; cache engineering keeps the text history and drops only selected KV entries, reusing retained states without recomputation. Nested color blocks show that retained KV can still carry information from dropped history.](figs/2610.28577/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: re-prefill cost versus accuracy

Longer agent trajectories cause two KV-cache problems. On cost, retaining and repeatedly reading accumulated cache incurs heavy storage and I/O overhead. On accuracy, performance drops sharply once the number of attended KV states or their positional range exceeds what the model handles reliably.

Context engineering shrinks the cache by trimming or summarizing old messages, but the earlier the edit, the longer the suffix that must be re-prefilled. Common harnesses therefore wait until the active context hits a threshold, then trim or summarize most of the trajectory at once and keep only the last few rounds so recomputation stays short. Such abrupt cuts tend to lose useful information from intermediate rounds. The authors test GPT-OSS-120B on the first 100 BrowseComp-Plus (BCP) tasks (four trials each, at most 100 rounds): trim-based context engineering that keeps only the latest 12 tool responses costs 1.85× the full-context baseline, and summarization at a 48K threshold cuts cost by about 7% but loses 5 points of accuracy. Dropping older tool-response cache directly improves accuracy and reduces cost at the same time.

## 2. Method: three cache operations

Cache engineering separates two lengths: the trajectory's **logical token length** and the size of the **active cache** that takes part in later attention. Context engineering edits the logical sequence; cache engineering edits only the active cache. The paper defines three operations:

- **append**: the standard cache update; it processes a new token, appends its KV entry and advances the position index by one.
- **drop(P)**: excludes the KV entries at indices $P$ from later attention while leaving retained states, their position encodings and the logical sequence unchanged. Drop does not change the position index used by later appends.
- **repos**: re-indexes the $r$ retained entries to positions $0,\ldots,r-1$ in logical order, and the next token starts at $r$. For RoPE, moving a key from position $p$ to $q$ is just $K\leftarrow R(q)R(p)^{-1}K$; values are untouched and nothing is recomputed.

Repos is needed because drop does not reset the position index. Even with a small cache, indices keep growing with the logical trajectory and eventually hit the model's position limit.

To choose what to keep, the authors look at attention patterns: older tokens get less attention than recent ones, and at similar relative positions tool responses get less attention than assistant messages. The main policy is therefore **tool-response rolling drop**: keep all reasoning and the latest $K$ tool responses ($K=12$ in the experiments), and progressively drop older tool-response cache.

## 3. The core challenge: cache state depends on history

With standard KV caching, the token prefix uniquely determines the cached state, so prefix matching suffices for reuse. Cache engineering breaks this: **the same token sequence under different operation sequences yields different cache states**.

![Cache operation trajectories and history-dependent KV states. (a) ① appends C after A and B, then drops A; ② drops A before appending C; ③ starts from B alone and appends C. All three retain B and C. (b) B's KV is identical in ① and ② but differs in ③; C's KV differs in all three. (c) The extended radix tree shares the A–B prefix of ① and ②, then branches on the timing of the drop.](figs/2610.28577/hf5.png)

Take the example: all three trajectories retain B and C, but in ① C was computed while A was visible, in ② C cannot see A, and in ③ B itself has no prefix. C's KV therefore differs in all three. The paper uses a **cache operation sequence** $o_{1:m}$ to describe state precisely: for a fixed model, starting from an empty cache, this sequence uniquely determines the current cache. The serving system must track both token history and operation history to reuse correctly.

## 4. The AKV serving system

AKV follows the principle of a stateless interface with stateful serving. The interface keeps the standard chat API: the messages field gives the full logical sequence as usual (each message implies an append), and a new optional cache field specifies drop and reposition with an "operate after message i" grammar. Clients need not know which KV states remain on the server; each round they simply extend the messages and operations as they normally would.

Internally, cache management preserves three properties: reuse only when states are equivalent; reclaim unused cache without breaking request isolation; restore evicted states in one prefill pass. Three mechanisms provide them:

- **Extended radix tree (reuse)**: when a request drops cache, a drop node recording the dropped indices is inserted at the trigger point on its path. Prefix matching compares both tokens and operations, so ① and ② share the A–B prefix but each keep their own C because they drop A at different times. Repos creates a new positional version by copying cache and rotating keys, forming a new branch with a reposition node; matching position indices allow direct reuse, differing ones require key rotation.
- **Drop-aware eviction**: an entry becomes evictable only when no ongoing computation or restoration needs it. For example, once both ① and ② have dropped A, its cache can be freed before the requests finish. Dropped cache is evicted before cache from completed requests, which is more likely to be reused next round. Positional versions are evicted independently.
- **Segment-batch attention (restore)**: ordinary causal prefill cannot reproduce states shaped by drop and repos, and replaying them step by step needs many forward passes. At each layer, AKV splits queries at drop and repos trigger points; each segment attends causally to its own tokens and to cache from earlier segments that is still active, while dropped cache stays visible to the earlier segments that originally used it. Only attention is segmented; the FFN still processes the whole batch once, avoiding repeated FFN weight reads per segment. Segments needing different positions get temporary KV versions built by rotating keys and copying values.

## 5. Experiments

The baselines are two summarization-based context-engineering schemes. **Standard** uses a higher, model-specific threshold (96K for GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7, 192K for MiroThinker-1.7-Mini); **Text Engineering** uses the same policy with a 48K threshold for all models. AKV uses rolling drop that keeps the latest 12 tool responses, with the repos threshold equal to Standard's summarization threshold. Benchmarks are BCP, xbench-DeepSearch-2510, the 103-task text-only GAIA validation subset and SWE-bench Verified. Cost is computed from active input and generated tokens; to be conservative, every repositioned token is also charged at the cache-hit rate, deliberately overestimating key-rotation cost.

**Task performance and cost (average over four benchmarks; score is pass rate %, cost in US cents per task):**

| Model | Standard score / cost | Text Eng. score / cost | AKV score / cost |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| MiniMax-M2.7 | 52.4 / 5.0 | 52.8 / 5.7 | 53.7 / 4.4 |
| GPT-OSS-120B | 51.0 / 11.2 | 48.3 / 10.2 | 53.1 / 7.3 |
| MiroThinker-1.7-Mini | 44.1 / 20.4 | 37.1 / 18.1 | 45.8 / 14.8 |

AKV has the highest average score on all three models, 1.3–2.1 points above Standard and 0.9–8.7 above Text Engineering, and its average cost is 27.7% below Standard and 21.9% below Text Engineering. It does not win every cell: on MiniMax-M2.7, Text Engineering is higher on BCP (62.3 vs 58.9) and Standard is higher on SWE-Verified (75.2 vs 74.4).

Where the accuracy gain comes from: on the first 100 BCP tasks with GPT-OSS-120B, all three methods are comparable below 48K logical tokens; Text Engineering is lowest in the 48–96K range and Standard is lowest above 96K, matching their respective summarization thresholds. This fits the explanation that abrupt cuts lose information, whereas rolling drop removes older tool responses gradually.

**Serving efficiency** (eight A800-80GB GPUs, four for prefill and four for decode, TP=4, Top-80 SWE-Verified): at each method's peak-throughput setting, AKV (concurrency 14) achieves 1.36× and 1.51× speedups in mean and P95 latency over Standard (concurrency 12), with 1.53× input and 1.18× output throughput. At concurrency 14 and 16, KV pressure increases Standard's re-prefill work, and its P95 latency reaches 229.90 s at concurrency 16 against 30.63 s for AKV. The latency breakdown shows the decode speedup comes mainly from less full-attention time: a shorter active context means fewer KV reads and less attention compute per step.

![GPT-OSS-120B on SWE-bench Verified: (a) online evaluation on the first 100 tasks, cumulative pass rate versus GPU hours, where AKV reaches the highest final pass rate in the least GPU time; (b) cumulative pass rate versus cumulative logical input tokens over 500 tasks; (c) serving throughput versus concurrency.](figs/2610.28577/hf8.png)

**Ablations and policy exploration** (GPT-OSS-120B, first 100 tasks per benchmark): dropping tool responses without repos gives 55.0 on BCP; adding repos raises it to 62.0, because exploration can continue instead of halting at the position limit. With repos enabled, dropping reasoning cache, alone or together with tool responses, is worse on both benchmarks than dropping tool responses alone; on SWE they score 36.5 and 34.5 against 41.0. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) uses MiniMax-M2.7 to refine policies on 20 BCP tasks and evaluates them on 100 held-out tasks; the policies from iterations 3 and 6 keep Standard's accuracy while cutting per-task cost by 15.6% and 17.8% relative to Standard. When cache management is exposed as a tool for the agent to decide, GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7 reach 61.0% and 64.0% on a BCP subset; cost falls from 13.4 to 12.1 cents for the former and rises from 5.4 to 5.9 cents for the latter, which runs more turns.

## 6. Limitations and what it means in practice

The authors list as future work further exploration of cache-engineering strategies, training agents under this scheme, and serving support for linear-attention models. A Tsinghua team proposes cache engineering: leave the text trajectory untouched, drop selected entries directly from the active KV cache, and reuse what remains as is. With its serving system AKV, a simple tool-response rolling-drop policy across three models and four agent benchmarks raises average scores by 1.7 points and cuts average cost by 27.7% relative to conventional threshold-triggered summarization, with 1.18× output throughput and a 1.51× speedup in P95 request latency.

Longer agent trajectories cause two KV-cache problems. On cost, retaining and repeatedly reading accumulated cache incurs heavy storage and I/O overhead. On accuracy, performance drops sharply once the number of attended KV states or their positional range exceeds what the model handles reliably.

Context engineering shrinks the cache by trimming or summarizing old messages, but the earlier the edit, the longer the suffix that must be re-prefilled. Common harnesses therefore wait until the active context hits a threshold, then trim or summarize most of the trajectory at once and keep only the last few rounds so recomputation stays short. Such abrupt cuts tend to lose useful information from intermediate rounds. The authors test GPT-OSS-120B on the first 100 BrowseComp-Plus (BCP) tasks (four trials each, at most 100 rounds): trim-based context engineering that keeps only the latest 12 tool responses costs 1.85× the full-context baseline, and summarization at a 48K threshold cuts cost by about 7% but loses 5 points of accuracy. Dropping older tool-response cache directly improves accuracy and reduces cost at the same time.

2. Method: three cache operations

Cache engineering separates two lengths: the trajectory's logical token length and the size of the active cache that takes part in later attention. Context engineering edits the logical sequence; cache engineering edits only the active cache. The paper defines three operations:

  • append: the standard cache update; it processes a new token, appends its KV entry and advances the position index by one.
  • drop(P): excludes the KV entries at indices P from later attention while leaving retained states, their position encodings and the logical sequence unchanged. Drop does not change the position index used by later appends.
  • repos: re-indexes the r retained entries to positions 0,…,r−1 in logical order, and the next token starts at r. For RoPE, moving a key from position p to q is just K←R(q)R(p)−1K; values are untouched and nothing is recomputed.

Repos is needed because drop does not reset the position index. Even with a small cache, indices keep growing with the logical trajectory and eventually hit the model's position limit.

To choose what to keep, the authors look at attention patterns: older tokens get less attention than recent ones, and at similar relative positions tool responses get less attention than assistant messages. The main policy is therefore tool-response rolling drop: keep all reasoning and the latest K tool responses ($K=12$ in the experiments), and progressively drop older tool-response cache.

3. The core challenge: cache state depends on history

With standard KV caching, the token prefix uniquely determines the cached state, so prefix matching suffices for reuse. Cache engineering breaks this: the same token sequence under different operation sequences yields different cache states.

Take the example: all three trajectories retain B and C, but in ① C was computed while A was visible, in ② C cannot see A, and in ③ B itself has no prefix. C's KV therefore differs in all three. The paper uses a cache operation sequence o1:m​ to describe state precisely: for a fixed model, starting from an empty cache, this sequence uniquely determines the current cache. The serving system must track both token history and operation history to reuse correctly.

4. The AKV serving system

AKV follows the principle of a stateless interface with stateful serving. The interface keeps the standard chat API: the messages field gives the full logical sequence as usual (each message implies an append), and a new optional cache field specifies drop and reposition with an "operate after message i" grammar. Clients need not know which KV states remain on the server; each round they simply extend the messages and operations as they normally would.

Internally, cache management preserves three properties: reuse only when states are equivalent; reclaim unused cache without breaking request isolation; restore evicted states in one prefill pass. Three mechanisms provide them:

  • Extended radix tree (reuse): when a request drops cache, a drop node recording the dropped indices is inserted at the trigger point on its path. Prefix matching compares both tokens and operations, so ① and ② share the A–B prefix but each keep their own C because they drop A at different times. Repos creates a new positional version by copying cache and rotating keys, forming a new branch with a reposition node; matching position indices allow direct reuse, differing ones require key rotation.
  • Drop-aware eviction: an entry becomes evictable only when no ongoing computation or restoration needs it. For example, once both ① and ② have dropped A, its cache can be freed before the requests finish. Dropped cache is evicted before cache from completed requests, which is more likely to be reused next round. Positional versions are evicted independently.
  • Segment-batch attention (restore): ordinary causal prefill cannot reproduce states shaped by drop and repos, and replaying them step by step needs many forward passes. At each layer, AKV splits queries at drop and repos trigger points; each segment attends causally to its own tokens and to cache from earlier segments that is still active, while dropped cache stays visible to the earlier segments that originally used it. Only attention is segmented; the FFN still processes the whole batch once, avoiding repeated FFN weight reads per segment. Segments needing different positions get temporary KV versions built by rotating keys and copying values.

papers.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
papers.abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.
papers.authors: Sahil Joshi, Prithvi Dixit, Aryan Katiyar, Agniva Chowdhury, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Anshumali Shrivastava, Aditya Desai, Kumar Krishna Agrawal

papers.summary: Long-context decode is bottlenecked by a growing KV cache; sparse attention’s deterministic top-k drops residual mass, sampling adds variance, and hybrids still lag dense. Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA) allocates the sparse budget by strata to close the sparse–dense gap at extreme sparsity: at 50× sparsity it lifts the strongest practical baseline from 81.8%→84.2% at 32K and 63.8%→69.3% at 128K, recovering 94% and 85% of dense performance; decode vs FlashInfer reaches up to 2.96× at 1M context. ==At extreme sparsity, stratify to recover residual attention mass—do not only chase top-k==.

deep_reading.content:
In long-context decoding, every new token reads the whole KV cache from HBM, so attention cost grows linearly with context. Sparse attention reads only a fraction of it, but at aggressive settings such as 50× sparsity, current methods remain far from dense attention: on RULER-HARD at 32K, Llama-3.1-8B scores 88.76 with dense attention and only 72.51 with PQCache-style top-k. This paper proposes Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA): ==keep high-scoring tokens deterministically, importance-sample the remaining tail by proxy scores, and correct the weights by inclusion probabilities==. At the same 50× sparsity, Llama-3.1-8B rises to 83.67; on AIME 2025 with Qwen3.5-9B, SSA scores 59.8 against 36.7 for PQ. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA's decode attention is 2.96× faster than FlashInfer at 1M context.

![The SSA algorithm: proxy scores split tokens into a "heavy" stratum (kept deterministically) and a "residual" stratum; residual tokens are sampled by proxy score and deduplicated, each selected token is weighted by the inverse of its inclusion probability, and exact attention is computed over the selected set.](figs/2610.28441/hf5.png)

## 1. The problem: top-k drops the tail, uniform sampling wastes the budget

There are three existing ways to spend a sparse-attention budget $k$. **Deterministic retrieval** (Quest, PQCache, and Tactic for top-p) picks the highest-scoring tokens by proxy score. It works when attention is concentrated, but when attention is diffuse or long-tailed, all mass outside the set is lost, especially when proxy errors push genuinely important tokens just below the cutoff. **Pure sampling** (MagicPig) uses LSH-based sampling with importance correction; coverage is broader, but variance is high at small budgets. **Hybrid methods** (vAttention) keep the top-k and sample the rest uniformly. This beats both, yet a clear gap to dense attention remains at aggressive sparsity.

The authors' preliminary study pins down the flaw in uniform sampling: residual attention mass is very unevenly distributed, and uniform sampling spends as much budget on tokens that contribute almost nothing as on the rest. Figure 1 shows that score-guided importance sampling has consistently lower relative $L_2$ error than uniform sampling.

![Left: relative L2 error at 50× sparsity as the top-k:sampling budget split varies. Right: error as sparsity varies with a fixed 3:2 split. Score-guided sampling stays below uniform sampling throughout.](figs/2610.28441/hf1.png)

## 2. Method: stratify, sample, then correct

First, recall importance-sampled sparse attention. Let $s_i=\mathbf q^\top\mathbf k_i/\sqrt d$ and $w_i=\exp(s_i)$. If each token enters the set $\mathcal S$ with probability $\pi_i$, weight it by $1/\pi_i$:

$$\widehat{\mathbf o}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(w_i/\pi_i)\mathbf v_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}w_i/\pi_i}$$

This is inverse-probability weighting: a token that was unlikely to be chosen gets a larger weight when it is chosen, standing in for similar tokens that were not. SSA has three steps.

**Step 1: allocate the budget from proxy scores.** Apply softmax to the proxy scores $\tilde s_i$ (from PQCache's product quantization in the experiments) to get $q_i$, and find $\lambda$ such that $\sum_i\min\{1,\lambda q_i\}=k$. Tokens with $\lambda q_i\ge1$ form the heavy set $\mathcal H$ and are kept deterministically; the remaining budget $m=k-|\mathcal H|$ goes to sampling the residual set $\mathcal R$. The heavy-set size is not hand-set; the proxy distribution decides it, and a sharper distribution yields a larger heavy set.

**Step 2: score-guided sampling of the residual.** Renormalize $q_i$ over $\mathcal R$ into a proposal $p_i$, draw $m$ times with replacement, and deduplicate to get $\mathcal S$. A residual token's probability of being drawn at least once is $\pi_i=1-(1-p_i)^m$; heavy tokens have $\pi_i=1$.

**Step 3: exact scoring and correction.** Compute exact scores $\ell_i$ only for tokens in $\mathcal H\cup\mathcal S$, weight them by $\exp(\ell_i)/\pi_i$, and take the normalized weighted sum. Because repeated draws count once, at most $k$ tokens are read.

An illustrative walk-through (numbers are illustrative): a 1M-token context at 50× sparsity gives $k=20{,}000$. Suppose 8,000 tokens satisfy $\lambda q_i\ge1$; they enter the heavy set directly. The other 12,000 draws are made over about 990,000 residual tokens according to $p_i$. A token with small $p_i$ that is drawn carries a large $1/\pi_i$, representing a broad tail of similarly low-scoring tokens whose combined attention mass is still significant. Pure top-k drops this tail entirely; uniform sampling wastes most draws on tokens with near-zero weight.

The framework contains earlier methods as special cases: a heavy set alone is top-k or top-p; an empty heavy set is pure sampling; a uniform proposal gives the vAttention-style hybrid.

**Error bound.** Let $A_{\mathcal R}$ be the true attention mass in the residual set, and $\rho=\max_{i\in\mathcal R}\bar a_i/p_i$ measure how well the proposal covers the true residual mass ($\rho\ge1$, with equality when the two match). Theorem 2 shows that with probability at least $1-\delta$, the output error $\|\widehat{\mathbf o}-\mathbf o\|_2$ scales as $A_{\mathcal R}\rho/\sqrt m$, with deduplication contributing only a constant factor. This states the allocation trade-off directly: keeping more heavy tokens lowers $A_{\mathcal R}$, leaving more sampling budget raises $m$, and a proxy that underestimates an important residual token raises $\rho$ and the error.

## 3. Core contribution

The main contribution is unifying retrieval and sampling in one framework, **in which a single proxy score decides who is kept, who is sampled and how weights are corrected**. It is orthogonal to the choice of approximate retrieval: any top-k method that yields proxy scores (PQCache, Quest and others) can serve as SSA's proposal, so improvements in retrieval carry straight over to SSA. The second contribution is engineering: sampling is often assumed too slow, and the authors' kernels show it can beat dense attention at long context.

## 4. Implementation: keeping sampling off the critical path

For efficiency, the real kernel uses a fixed heavy fraction $h$ instead of adaptive allocation; the authors report that this fixed-budget variant closely matches the theoretical one. A decode step has four stages; the first three scan the whole context but read only a few bytes per token.

- **Proxy scoring**: each key is a 16-byte PQ code (16 subspaces, 256 centroids), versus 1 KiB for its fp16 KV pair at head dimension 256. A lookup table computes proxy scores for all tokens, and the same kernel masks sink and local tokens.
- **Heavy-set selection**: radix top-k returns an unordered index set, since the estimator does not depend on order.
- **Residual sampling**: a hierarchical sampler picks a 1024-token chunk, then a 32-token sub-tile, then one token among at most 32. A per-row hash table removes duplicates. $\pi_i$ is clamped at $10^{-4}$ to avoid huge weights, at the cost of a small bias. A counter-based RNG keeps samples fresh across replays while remaining compatible with CUDA graph capture.
- **Sparse decode**: the selected K and V are gathered from the paged KV cache and evaluated with online softmax, splitting each query head across thread blocks and merging with log-sum-exp. At 1M context and batch 1, 64 splits are 1.58–1.71× faster than 32; 128 or 256 splits are slower.

## 5. Experiments

Baselines are Oracle-top-k (exact scores for top-k selection; it cannot accelerate anything and serves as an upper reference for deterministic retrieval), PQCache and vAttention (PQ), all with 128 sink and 128 local tokens. Models are Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-4B/9B and Ministral-3-3B/8B, plus Qwen3.5-27B on LongBench.

**RULER-HARD at 50× sparsity.** SSA beats PQ and vAttention (PQ) for every model and length. All three use the same PQ scores and budget; only the allocation differs.

| Model | Length | Dense | PQ | vAttn (PQ) | Oracle-top-k | SSA |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Llama-3.1-8B | 32K | 88.76 | 72.51 | 66.71 | 78.80 | 83.67 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | 128K | 71.26 | 39.73 | 39.45 | 56.10 | 47.53 |
| Ministral-3-3B | 32K | 86.69 | 70.81 | 69.26 | 72.81 | 82.05 |
| Ministral-3-8B | 32K | 89.33 | 81.83 | 78.69 | 86.61 | 84.17 |
| Ministral-3-8B | 128K | 81.45 | 62.99 | 63.78 | 75.83 | 69.25 |

On Ministral-3-8B, SSA recovers 94% and 85% of dense performance at 32K and 128K. Oracle-top-k is still stronger at 128K on Llama and Ministral-3-3B, and at every length on Ministral-3-8B, which suggests proxy-score quality remains the bottleneck. On Qwen3.5, every sparse method stays within two points of dense.

**AIME 2025 (32K-token generations).** SSA's lead grows with sparsity. On Qwen3.5-9B (dense 66.3) at 50×, SSA scores 59.8 against 48.3 for Oracle-top-k, 36.7 for PQ and 35.8 for vAttention (PQ); at 100×, SSA still has 51.5 while vAttention (PQ) falls to 3.5. Low sparsity is different: at 5×, vAttention (PQ) is better (65.4 vs 61.0). An ablation on the heavy fraction $h$ shows that hybrid splits with $h\in[0.2,0.8]$ reach 61.0–64.0, against 40.2–42.5 for pure sampling ($h=0$) and 49.4–53.8 for pure top-k ($h=1$).

**LOFT and LongBench.** On LOFT, SSA has the lowest attention error among non-oracle methods at every length and sparsity, but the task metric (subspan-EM) differs by at most 0.04 across methods. On LongBench with Qwen3.5-27B, all sparse methods are within one point of dense. Lower error does not always turn into a task-score difference.

**Decode efficiency.** Measured on one H200 (16 query heads, 4 KV heads, head dimension 256, fp16 KV). At batch 1 and 128K, SSA runs at only 0.60–0.74× FlashInfer's speed; as context grows the overhead amortizes, and at 1M it is 1.79×, 1.39× and 1.07× faster at 50×, 20× and 10× sparsity. Gains grow with batch size, reaching 2.96× at 1M, batch 16 and 50×. Kernel optimization matters most at batch 1: an unoptimized reference runs at 0.37–0.47× FlashInfer, and the optimizations improve it 2.95–3.80×. The two-level sampler is 1.21–3.16× faster than chunk-only sampling, keeping sampling at 0.30–1.18 ms at 1M context and $h=0.4$.

![Decode attention speedup on one H200: (a) at batch 1, SSA overtakes FlashInfer beyond 256K and reaches 1.79× at 1M and 50× sparsity; (b) at 1M context, speedup grows with batch size to 2.96× at batch 16; (c) overhead of two-level residual sampling relative to chunk-only sampling as the number of draws grows.](figs/2610.28441/hf4.png)

## 6. Limitations and what it means in practice

There are several limitations. The real kernel uses a fixed heavy fraction, and an efficient adaptive implementation is future work. Clamping $\pi_i$ introduces a small bias. Sampling makes outputs stochastic, so two decodes of the same request do not produce identical attention, and settings that need reproducibility should fix the seed. Below 128K at batch 1, SSA is slower than FlashInfer. Where sparsity barely hurts anyway, as with Qwen3.5 or LongBench, SSA shows no clear advantage. The authors' stated next step is to make SSA verifiable, with user-set guarantees on approximation quality.

For industry, the fit is clear: **million-token contexts, decode serving at larger batch sizes, and sparsity pushed beyond 20–50×**, such as long-horizon agent histories, very long document QA or long reasoning chains. If your system already runs a top-k retriever such as PQCache or Quest, adopting SSA only means moving part of the budget from top-k to proxy-guided sampling and adding the $1/\pi_i$ correction; the retrieval index can be reused as is. Before deploying, sweep $h$ on your own tasks: the AIME results show $h$ anywhere in 0.2–0.8 works well, while pure top-k and pure sampling are clearly worse. ==If your sparsity is only 5–10×, existing top-k or vAttention may already be enough==; SSA's gains come mainly in the aggressive regime.

Error bound. Let AR​ be the true attention mass in the residual set, and ρ=maxi∈R​aˉi​/pi​ measure how well the proposal covers the true residual mass (ρ≥1, with equality when the two match). Theorem 2 shows that with probability at least 1−δ, the output error ∥o−o∥2​ scales as AR​ρ/m​, with deduplication contributing only a constant factor. This states the allocation trade-off directly: keeping more heavy tokens lowers AR​, leaving more sampling budget raises m, and a proxy that underestimates an important residual token raises ρ and the error.

3. Core contribution

The main contribution is unifying retrieval and sampling in one framework, in which a single proxy score decides who is kept, who is sampled and how weights are corrected. It is orthogonal to the choice of approximate retrieval: any top-k method that yields proxy scores (PQCache, Quest and others) can serve as SSA's proposal, so improvements in retrieval carry straight over to SSA. The second contribution is engineering: sampling is often assumed too slow, and the authors' kernels show it can beat dense attention at long context.

4. Implementation: keeping sampling off the critical path

For efficiency, the real kernel uses a fixed heavy fraction h instead of adaptive allocation; the authors report that this fixed-budget variant closely matches the theoretical one. A decode step has four stages; the first three scan the whole context but read only a few bytes per token.

  • Proxy scoring: each key is a 16-byte PQ code (16 subspaces, 256 centroids), versus 1 KiB for its fp16 KV pair at head dimension 256. A lookup table computes proxy scores for all tokens, and the same kernel masks sink and local tokens.
  • Heavy-set selection: radix top-k returns an unordered index set, since the estimator does not depend on order.
  • Residual sampling: a hierarchical sampler picks a 1024-token chunk, then a 32-token sub-tile, then one token among at most 32. A per-row hash table removes duplicates. πi​ is clamped at 10−4 to avoid huge weights, at the cost of a small bias. A counter-based RNG keeps samples fresh across replays while remaining compatible with CUDA graph capture.
  • Sparse decode: the selected K and V are gathered from the paged KV cache and evaluated with online softmax, splitting each query head across thread blocks and merging with log-sum-exp. At 1M context and batch 1, 64 splits are 1.58–1.71× faster than 32; 128 or 256 splits are slower.

5. Experiments

Baselines are Oracle-top-k (exact scores for top-k selection; it cannot accelerate anything and serves as an upper reference for deterministic retrieval), PQCache and vAttention (PQ), all with 128 sink and 128 local tokens. Models are Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-4B/9B and Ministral-3-3B/8B, plus Qwen3.5-27B on LongBench.

RULER-HARD at 50× sparsity. SSA beats PQ and vAttention (PQ) for every model and length. All three use the same PQ scores and budget; only the allocation differs.

On Ministral-3-8B, SSA recovers 94% and 85% of dense performance at 32K and 128K. Oracle-top-k is still stronger at 128K on Llama and Ministral-3-3B, and at every length on Ministral-3-8B, which suggests proxy-score quality remains the bottleneck. On Qwen3.5, every sparse method stays within two points of dense.

AIME 2025 (32K-token generations). SSA's lead grows with sparsity. On Qwen3.5-9B (dense 66.3) at 50×, SSA scores 59.8 against 48.3 for Oracle-top-k, 36.7 for PQ and 35.8 for vAttention (PQ); at 100×, SSA still has 51.5 while vAttention (PQ) falls to 3.5. Low sparsity is different: at 5×, vAttention (PQ) is better (65.4 vs 61.0). An ablation on the heavy fraction h shows that hybrid splits with h∈[0.2,0.8] reach 61.0–64.0, against 40.2–42.5 for pure sampling ($h=0$) and 49.4–53.8 for pure top-k ($h=1$).

LOFT and LongBench. On LOFT, SSA has the lowest attention error among non-oracle methods at every length and sparsity, but the task metric (subspan-EM) differs by at most 0.04 across methods. On LongBench with Qwen3.5-27B, all sparse methods are within one point of dense. Lower error does not always turn into a task-score difference.

Decode efficiency. Measured on one H200 (16 query heads, 4 KV heads, head dimension 256, fp16 KV). At batch 1 and 128K, SSA runs at only 0.60–0.74× FlashInfer's speed; as context grows the overhead amortizes, and at 1M it is 1.79×, 1.39× and 1.07× faster at 50×, 20× and 10× sparsity. Gains grow with batch size, reaching 2.96× at 1M, batch 16 and 50×. Kernel optimization matters most at batch 1: an unoptimized reference runs at 0.37–0.47× FlashInfer, and the optimizations improve it 2.95–3.80×. The two-level sampler is 1.21–3.16× faster than chunk-only sampling, keeping sampling at 0.30–1.18 ms at 1M context and $h=0.4$.

6. Limitations and what it means in practice

There are several limitations. The real kernel uses a fixed heavy fraction, and an efficient adaptive implementation is future work. Clamping πi​ introduces a small bias. Sampling makes outputs stochastic, so two decodes of the same request do not produce identical attention, and settings that need reproducibility should fix the seed. Below 128K at batch 1, SSA is slower than FlashInfer. Where sparsity barely hurts anyway, as with Qwen3.5 or LongBench, SSA shows no clear advantage. The authors' stated next step is to make SSA verifiable, with user-set guarantees on approximation quality.

For industry, the fit is clear: million-token contexts, decode serving at larger batch sizes, and sparsity pushed beyond 20–50×, such as long-horizon agent histories, very long document QA or long reasoning chains. If your system already runs a top-k retriever such as PQCache or Quest, adopting SSA only means moving part of the budget from top-k to proxy-guided sampling and adding the 1/πi​ correction; the retrieval index can be reused as is. Before deploying, sweep h on your own tasks: the AIME results show h anywhere in 0.2–0.8 works well, while pure top-k and pure sampling are clearly worse. If your sparsity is only 5–10×, existing top-k or vAttention may already be enough; SSA's gains come mainly in the aggressive regime.

papers.title: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 2
papers.abstract: The Global Performance Tuner is a feature for automatic performance tuning released in NVIDIA TensorRT 11.1. It provides automatic, accuracy-aware and end-to-end performance tuning within TensorRT by customizing different optimizations for different models. This post, Part 2, uses the notation from Part 1 to describe the algorithm and architectural design of the Global Performance Tuner feature. It also provides best practices for using it.

papers.title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders
papers.authors: Hyojung Han, Ryangkyung Kang, Youngeun Kim, Seung-Hun Jeon
papers.abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cos
